name: Real-time & Communication
shortDescription: Group chat in temporary rooms, with real-time messages and its own login.
description: Group chat in temporary rooms, with its own login and messages arriving in real time.
longDescription: A group chat built around temporary rooms: create an account, join or create a room via a link, and chat with up to 10 people in real time. Every room expires on its own 7 days after creation, with nothing left behind.
tags: Realtime, Chat, WebSocket, Server-Sent Events, Java, Spring Boot, Redis, JWT
architecture: Next.js frontend consuming an external Java API, WebSocket over STOMP for the room chat, Server-Sent Events for closed-room notifications, short-lived access JWT with a rotating refresh token, cross-origin session cookie, room expiry driven by a database timestamp — not a token
technologies: Java 21, Spring Boot, Spring WebSocket (STOMP), Spring Security, JJWT, PostgreSQL (Supabase), Redis, BCrypt, Server-Sent Events
concepts: WebSocket lifecycle, STOMP protocol, Redis Pub/Sub across instances, online presence via TTL, JWT with rotating refresh tokens, cross-origin session cookies, data expiry via scheduled job, relational modeling of rooms and members
overviewParagraph1: WebSocket and Server-Sent Events (SSE) power a bunch of things you already use every day without noticing: a live game score updating on its own, a delivery tracker moving across a map, a website's support chat, a notification landing on your phone without you refreshing anything.
overviewParagraph2: The clearest way to show how that works in practice is with what these technologies do best: a chat. Chat rooms have been around since the earliest internet forums, and they're still in everyone's pocket today, inside apps like WhatsApp and Discord.
overviewParagraph3: Most of them solve that communication in two complementary ways: a channel that keeps the conversation open in real time while you're in it, and a quick heads-up for when you're not. That's exactly what this demo shows: you create an account, join a room through a link, and exchange messages with other people in real time — seeing both sides of that real-time communication at work.
websocketParagraph1: Born in 2011, when it became an official internet standard (RFC 6455) — after a few years running as an experiment inside the wave of additions known as HTML5.
websocketParagraph2: The connection starts as a normal HTTP GET request, but it carries special headers: Connection: Upgrade, Upgrade: websocket, and a random key (Sec-WebSocket-Key). The server replies with a 101 Switching Protocols status, confirming that key.
websocketParagraph3: From that point on, the conversation stops being HTTP. There's no more GET, POST, or PUT involved — what flows from here on is WebSocket's own protocol, over the same TCP connection that was already open.
websocketParagraph4: How the server knows who's who: the TCP connection itself, kept open the whole time, is the identity. During the handshake — that initial GET — the server reads a session cookie or token sent along with the request, and ties that specific socket to a user, keeping that mapping in memory. After that, no message needs to re-identify itself: the socket alone already says who's talking.
websocketParagraph5: Once open, the connection becomes a two-way lane over the same pipe: both browser and server can write to it at any moment, without waiting to be asked. On the browser, that shows up as an event that fires whenever something arrives from the server; on the server, each connection has its own listener that fires whenever that specific client sends something.
websocketParagraph6: On the wire, after the handshake, what travels is no longer full HTTP requests — it's small binary frames, each one carrying a type flag, the payload length, and the payload itself. This runs over the exact same port and TCP connection the original request used (port 443 for wss://, encrypted the same way HTTPS is) — only the format of what flows through it changes.
websocketParagraph7: In a room with several people, the server keeps one independent open connection per person — picture a 5-person room as 5 open pipes at once, all arriving at the same server. When someone sends a message, it doesn't spread through the network on its own: the server receives it and writes it, one by one, into each of the other 4 open pipes in that room. That loop — writing into every connection in the room — is what makes the message reach everyone at the same time.
sseParagraph1: Unlike WebSocket, SSE doesn't invent a new protocol at all — it's plain HTTP, start to finish.
sseParagraph2: The browser makes a normal GET request, with an Accept: text/event-stream header, and the server replies with Content-Type: text/event-stream. The difference is that this response never finishes: the server keeps that same GET open indefinitely.
sseParagraph3: Client identity works exactly like any regular HTTP request: through a session cookie or token sent on that single initial GET. The server keeps that open response tied to a user — it's no longer a socket connection like WebSocket, it's an HTTP response the server simply decided not to close.
sseParagraph4: On the browser, the EventSource API listens to that response continuously and fires an event for every new chunk, with no need to ask again. But the flow only goes one way: the browser has no way to write back over that same connection. If the client needs to send something to the server, that's a separate, ordinary HTTP request — a regular POST, unrelated to the SSE channel itself.
sseParagraph5: On the wire, what keeps that "endless" response working is HTTP's own Transfer-Encoding: chunked — the server sends content in pieces, never declaring a total size or closing the connection. Each piece follows a simple text format, starting with "data: " and ending with two line breaks.
sseParagraph6: With multiple people connected, the server keeps one open HTTP response per person — each one is, in practice, a listen-only connection. To notify everyone at once, it loops through the list of open responses and writes the same chunk into each one — the same principle as WebSocket, a loop writing into every connection, except here each connection only ever receives, never talks back.
dailyLabel: WebSocket and SSE in everyday apps
dailyTitle: WebSocket and SSE in everyday apps
dailyIntegration: The two rarely compete — they usually complement each other. A conversation that needs two-way flow (you talk, the other person replies) calls for WebSocket. A heads-up that only needs to reach you, with no reply, calls for SSE. Most large apps use both at once, each one covering a different part of the product.
dailyExamples: That's the tooling behind WhatsApp, Telegram, and Discord delivering a message instantly, Facebook's and Twitter/X's feeds updating on their own, and iFood and Uber showing your order or your ride moving on the map in real time.
